title: Rescuer Handbook — Incident Scripting and Customer Lanes
author: Aisha N. Patel
content:
Overview

This handbook provides a compact, action-oriented playbook for first responders (the "Rescuers") when an incident threatens inference availability, latency SLOs, or customer traffic. It stitches together a three-phase rescue framework, runbook snippets, role-level responsibilities, customer communication lanes, status-page templates, and a reproducible postmortem skeleton. The document is designed to be used in-bridge, in-channel, and as the canonical handoff artifact after the incident.

Why this exists

- Reduce mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) and mean time to restore (MTTR) by giving on-call engineers a small set of deterministic actions.
- Standardize customer-facing messaging and escalation choices so legal/support/CS have consistent material.
- Make game days repeatable: this handbook doubles as a scenario catalog and scoring rubric.

Three-phase Rescue Framework (Detect → Stabilize → Recover)

1) Detect (0–5 minutes)
   - Primary signals: SLO burn rate alert, customer error-rate anomaly, region-level traffic drop, or control-plane API errors.
   - Quick checks (first 60s):
     • Check PagerDuty / Opsgenie alert details.
     • Confirm impacted service(s) in Alert payload (service name, region, model).
     • Open bridge (Slack channel or Zoom) and post a short header: who, what, where, severity.
   - Output: acknowledgment with a single-line hypothesis and list of immediate actions.

2) Stabilize (5–30 minutes)
   - Goal: stop customer-facing degradation and buy time for deeper debugging.
   - Standard stabilization actions (choose 1–3):
     • Shift traffic to healthy region/model variant via smart-routing: runbook command below.
     • Engage automatic fallback (model-variant downgrade) if configured for the route.
     • Scale up dedicated pool or enable burst capacity (Dedicated customers only).
     • Apply emergency rate limit (per-tenant) to prevent noisy neighbor effects.
     • Toggle feature flag that disables costly post-processing (e.g., reranker).
   - Evidence to collect: SLO dashboard snapshot, top-5 trace latencies, error-sample IDs, tenant list affected.

3) Recover (30–240 minutes)
   - Goal: restore normal routing and validate quality/metrics.
   - Recovery steps:
     1. Root-cause mitigation (fix config, restart degraded service, revert bad deploy).
     2. Ramp traffic back with canary (10% → 50% → 100%) monitoring latency and error rate windows (5m/1m).
     3. Post-restore sanity: run automated smoke tests across common prompts and sampling seeds.
     4. Prepare customer-facing resolution notice and credit assessment if SLO breached.

Role matrix and primary responsibilities

- Rescuer (first responder): own triage, stabilize actions, and evidence collection until handover.
- Bridge Operator: manage the communication channel, timestamp decisions, maintain timeline.
- Escalation Lead: senior engineer to own RCA and code-level fixes after stabilization.
- Customer Liaison (CS/SRE): draft customer-facing templates, coordinate credits, and capture affected tenants.

On-call rotation rules (quick reference)

- Shift length: 7×24: 12-hour primary window; 6pm–6am local clockwise rotation for region leads.
- Handoff: 10-minute warm handoff with the outgoing oncall including the state of open alerts and ongoing mitigations.
- Escalation timing:
  • Page acknowledged within 5 minutes.
  • If no ack within 10 minutes, escalate to Escalation Lead.
  • If incident remains unresolved for >4 hours, engage Director on call.
- Handover checklist (must be captured in the bridge channel):
  1. Current incident status and hypothesis.
  2. Actions taken and commands run.
  3. Remaining tasks and owners.
  4. Customer-impact note (tenants list, regions).

Rapid evidence checklist (first 30 minutes)

- Collect these before changing routing unless impossible:
  • SLO graph screenshots (token-latency, request-latency, error-rate).
  • Top traces (trace IDs) from APM for the window.
  • Controller logs (last 100 lines) and GPU node statuses.
  • KV cache eviction metrics and hit-rate deltas.
  • Recent deploys (git SHA and deployment time).
  • Tenant-specific request IDs and examples (for support).

Essential runbook commands (copy/paste ready)

- Shift traffic to standby region (example CLI, replace values):
  redwoodctl routing set --route inference-prod-uswest --enable-fallback --target-region us-east-1 --reason "emergency-stabilize"

- Disable a route temporarily: (non-destructive, time-limited)
  redwoodctl route update --id route-123 --state disabled --until "2026-03-02T14:30:00Z" --note "emergency disable; noisy neighbor"

- Apply tenant rate limit (API sample):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://admin.redwood/api/v1/tenants/tenant-abc/limits -d '{"qps":10,"reason":"incident-stabilize"}'

- Restart model-serving deployment (Kubernetes example):
  kubectl -n inference rollout restart deployment/serve-model-bert-quantized --record

- Snapshot logs for evidence:
  kubectl -n inference logs deployment/serve-model-bert-quantized --tail=200 > /tmp/bert-logs-$(date -u +%s).log

Customer communication lanes (templates and cadence)

We use three lanes dependent on impact and SLA tier. Each message should be short, empathetic, and include: incident id, short impact statement, what we are doing, expected next update time, and contact path.

Lane A — Major outage (SLO failure for >1 customer or platform-wide)
- Initial acknowledgement (within 30 minutes):
  Subject: [Incident {INC_ID}] Platform latency/degradation affecting inference – initial acknowledgement

  Body: "We are investigating an issue impacting Redwood Inference customers that may cause increased latency or failed requests for some workloads. Our on-call team has opened an incident (ID: {INC_ID}) and has begun mitigation steps (traffic rerouting and scaling). We will provide an update within 30 minutes. If you need immediate assistance, contact support@redwood.ai or your account manager."

- Update cadence: every 30–60 minutes while active.
- Resolution notice: include timeline, root cause summary, affected tenants, and credit assessment next-steps.

Lane B — Regional/tenant degradation (isolated customers)
- Initial acknowledgement (within 1 hour): similar template but include list of known affected tenant IDs and temporary workarounds (e.g., region switch).

Lane C — Informational / scheduled maintenance
- Pre-notice (72 hours before), reminder (24 hours), and post-complete confirmation.

Status page wording examples

- Status: Investigating (short): "We are investigating elevated request latency for model-gen routes in us-west-2. Some requests may time out. Incident ID: {INC_ID}."
- Status: Identified: "We have identified a partial outage caused by a configuration regression and are applying a rollback. Traffic is being shifted to us-east-1 to mitigate customer impact."
- Status: Monitoring: "A fix has been deployed and we are monitoring metrics for 30 minutes before returning to normal operation."
- Status: Resolved: "The issue is resolved as of {TIME_UTC}. We will publish a full postmortem within 72 hours."

Postmortem skeleton (publish within 72 hours - draft, final after RCA)

- Title: Incident {INC_ID}: one-line summary
- Severity: Sev1 | Sev2 | Sev3
- Date/time window: detection → resolution timestamps (UTC)
- Impact summary: tenants affected, estimated % of requests impacted, SLO delta, refunds/credits to be considered.
- Timeline: bullet list with timestamps and short entries (use bridge timeline as source).
- Root cause: one-paragraph technical description.
- Contributing factors: short bullets (deploy, config, autoscaling, testing gaps).
- Corrective actions (owner + due date): numbered list.
- Verification plan: how we measured success.
- Lessons learned + follow-ups (links to tasks/PRs).

Game day scenario: "Surge + config drift" (exercise)

Objective: validate stabilization steps and customer lanes for a model-serving config regression that causes increased latency and KV cache churn.

Setup steps for simulation team:
1. Inject config change into a canary with a flag that simulates 3× CPU for attention kernels.
2. Create synthetic tenants that generate 500 RPS each to simulate noisy neighbor.
3. Disable automatic fallback for the route to force manual decision-making.

Evaluation rubric (scored):
- Acknowledgement time (target <5m): 15 pts
- Stabilization within 20m: 25 pts
- Evidence collected and documented: 20 pts
- Proper customer lane messaging: 20 pts
- Postmortem published within 72h (draft): 20 pts

Runbook lifecycle and governance

- Runbooks referenced from this document must be reviewed every 6 months or after any incident where they were used.
- Every published runbook must include: owner, last runbook-executed timestamp, test-scenarios, and simulated run notes from the last game day.
- Deprecated steps must be appended with a comment and removed after 3 months of no references.

Appendix: quick-check templates

Bridge channel starter (copy/paste):
"BRIDGE OPEN — Incident {INC_ID}
- Lead: @{rescuer}
- Initial hypothesis: {short-hypothesis}
- Immediate actions: {action1}, {action2}
- Expected next update: {HH:MM UTC}
"

Customer initial acknowledgement (short):
"We are aware of an issue impacting inference requests in {region}. Our on-call team is actively investigating. Incident ID: {INC_ID}. Next update: {minutes} minutes. Signed — Redwood Inference Support"

Evidence capture checklist (copy/paste):
- SLO screenshot: /attachments/{INC_ID}/slo.png
- Top traces: [traceId1, traceId2]
- Deploy SHA: {sha}
- Commands executed: {list}

Contact and escalation directory (quick)

- Oncall Rescuer rotation: #eng-oncall (use PagerDuty to page primary)
- Escalation Lead: +1-555-0101 (on-call phone)
- Customer Liaison: cs@redwood.ai
